title: How to Show Appropriate Affection for Students
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that despite the fear created by news stories of teacher misconduct, showing affection for students is an essential part of motivating them and running a classroom well, because care is one of the three components of teacher credibility. He offers five practices to start: eye contact with a gentle smile, sparing and safe physical touch such as handshakes and fist bumps, quick moments of genuine connection, specific private encouragement, and writing down one appreciated thing about a student after each hour. He then names two things to stop, which are reducing kids to their worst behaviors and habitual complaining about them. The deeper claim is that affection depends on the teacher's own heart, so the internal work cannot be skipped. He closes by calling the love of one's students the hardest and most important part of the job.
points: Showing care is framed as a core classroom-management and motivation lever because care is part of teacher credibility.
Warmth is conveyed through concrete behaviors such as eye contact with a smile and boundaried touch like a handshake, fist bump, or sideways hug.
Specific private encouragement, naming what a student did and why it matters, beats vague public praise and also lifts the teacher out of a slump.
A daily written note of one thing appreciated per class hour trains the teacher to notice the positive in students.
Genuine affection requires internal work: stopping complaining and refusing to reduce students to their negative behaviors.
quotes: Despite the news stories (and the fear they create in well-meaning teachers like you and me who care for our students but are only ever one false allegation away from a damaged or ruined career), here’s the reality: showing affection for students is a powerful part of the work it takes to encourage student motivation and manage a classroom well.

The only thing I’d add is to smile while you’re looking a kid in the eyes. It doesn’t need to be big and goofy — a gentle smile will do — but when we look our kids in the eyes while smiling, we give them a nonverbal indicator that they matter, that they are heard and valued, that we care for them.
That doesn’t mean, however, that we should never touch! A simple handshake, fist bump, or high-five creates physical connection and shows affection.

I’m talking about any opportunity you see where a kid overcomes a challenge, does something better today than they did yesterday, engages with a hard-to-handle peer, or anything else that’s good. What you do when you see this is pull that student aside and simply say what you saw and why it matters.

What you’re doing with this discipline is training your heart and mind to latch onto the positive moments with your kids — the moments that remind you of the humanity that you share with them, of the reasons why you entered a profession that serves young people, of the reasons why this work is inherently good and noble.
If you want to maximally impact your students for their long-term good, then you’ve got to maximally impact your own heart. There’s no skipping the internal work.

Listen: if you sit and complain daily about your students, then it is a metaphysical impossibility for your heart to remain close to the work of seeking their long-term good. The human heart, under its own power, cannot act in love toward that which it despises.
